snip.t: Neurological: Numbness/tingling, gait instability, memory loss, mood change, depression, visual disturbances — Vitamin B12 deficiency (cobalamin) causes sub‑acute combined degeneration; folate deficiency may give mild neuro‑cognitive changes.
*Model answer*: Vitamin B12 deficiency – neurological signs (paresthesiae, loss of vibration) and macro‑ovalocytosis point to B12 rather than folate.
Neurological signs (paresthesias, gait ataxia): Vitamin B12 deficiency — Ileal disease or bacterial overgrowth consuming B12
Nutritional: Vitamin B12 deficiency, thiamine deficiency (Wernicke’s).
Posterior column – Romberg test; instability with eyes closed suggests dorsal column disease (vitamin B12 deficiency, HIV‑related myelopathy).
Metabolic / Nutritional: Diabetes mellitus, chronic alcohol excess, vitamin B12 deficiency, folate deficiency, thiamine deficiency (wet beri‑beri)

qs.q: A patient with an ileal resection develops severe vitamin B12 deficiency and bile salt malabsorption. Which specific transporter mechanism in the terminal ileum is disrupted by this surgical intervention?
qs.e: Bile salts are actively reabsorbed in the terminal ileum via a specialized apical sodium-dependent bile acid co-transporter.

qs.q: A 70-year-old man is diagnosed with severe vitamin B12 deficiency presenting with subacute combined cord degeneration. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment approach?
qs.e: Intramuscular hydroxocobalamin rapidly and reliably replenishes tissue stores and halts neurological progression in severe deficiency. Oral cyanocobalamin tablets are slower and less reliable when severe neurological deficits are present.

qs.q: Which of the following is a classic clinical feature of Vitamin B12 deficiency resulting from malabsorption?
o: Cheilosis along with painful atrophic glossitis
Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord
Tetany accompanied by a positive Chvostek sign
Follicular hyperkeratosis and severe night blindness
qs.e: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes macrocytic anemia and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, characterized by paresthesias, ataxia, and loss of vibratory sense. Tetany and positive Chvostek signs relate to calcium and Vitamin D deficiency.

qs.q: A patient with vitamin B12 deficiency develops bilateral numbness, tingling, and ataxia progressing to spastic weakness. Which spinal cord tracts are primarily affected?
o: Base of the pons and medullary pyramid fibers
Dorsal spinocerebellar tracts and ventral roots
Anterior spinothalamic and dorsal spinocerebellar tracts
Posterior columns and lateral corticospinal tracts
qs.e: Subacute combined degeneration involves the degeneration of both ascending posterior columns and descending lateral corticospinal tracts. Thiamine deficiency affects the mammillary bodies rather than primarily the spinal cord tracts.

qs.q: What is a major clinical risk if high doses of folic acid (>0.1 mg) are administered to a patient whose anemia is actually caused by an underlying vitamin B12 deficiency?
o: It invariably causes permanent gastrointestinal atresia
It might aggravate associated neurologic abnormalities
It may rapidly precipitate acute hemolytic crises
It will completely halt all bone marrow cellularity
qs.e: Doses of folate >0.1 mg can correct the anemia of vitamin B12 deficiency but might aggravate any associated neurologic abnormalities. Proper differential diagnosis is therefore vital before starting high-dose folate.

qs.q: A 52-year-old man with progressive fatigue is evaluated for suspected vitamin B12 deficiency. In the sequential evolution of cobalamin deficiency, which biochemical changes occur earliest in serum?
qs.e: Elevated serum methylmalonic acid and homocysteine levels develop early in cobalamin depletion before any rise in mean corpuscular volume or clinical anemia appears. Macrocytic anemia and cytopenias manifest much later in the disease process.

qs.q: Most common cause of vitamin B12 deficiency in Western countries?
o: Surgical removal of the gastric body
Chronic inflammation of the terminal ileum
qs.e: Autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor is the leading cause in Western populations.

qs.q: NOT a typical feature of vitamin B12 deficiency?
qs.e: B12 deficiency causes macrocytosis, plus unique neurological features (unlike folate deficiency).
